# Function Health (member biomarker-testing platform, US)

URL: https://www.functionhealth.com/

## Type system
- Display: `"Financier Display", Georgia, serif` — H1 80px/300, H2 64px/300.
  A light-weight editorial serif, with italic used for the key word in a
  headline ("check your **health**.") — the same italic-emphasis trick
  recurs across headings site-wide.
- Body/UI: `"FT Base", system-ui, sans-serif` at 16px/400 — a plain
  functional grotesk for everything that isn't a headline (nav, buttons,
  captions, table rows).
- No mono typeface used, despite the site being data-heavy — even the
  biomarker comparison table uses the sans body face, not a monospace
  numeric font.

## Color system
- bg: warm cream `#FEF9EF`, with a slightly deeper cream `#F5EEE1` for
  alternating sections.
- text: near-black warm grey `#2A2B2F`.
- surface/card: taupe `#DDD6CA`.
- accent: burnt terracotta `#B05A36` — used for CTA buttons, italic
  headline words, and the highlighted column in the biomarker comparison
  table.
- Pure black and white also appear in photography treatments and the
  footer.

## Layout & grid
- Wide hero (photography of a person in profile against warm cream) with
  serif headline overlapping the image edge.
- Content sections run in a centred ~1200px column; feature grids use 3-up
  and 2-up card layouts with soft-cream card backgrounds (never white on
  white).
- The signature "gold standard" comparison table is a dense
  multi-row/multi-column layout — the only place the site departs from
  generous whitespace to show real information density.

## Sections (order observed)
1. Full-bleed photographic hero (profile portrait) + serif headline +
   sticky top bar with plan pricing chips ("160+ lab tests," "Whole body
   scans," "$1 per day")
2. "Testing is easy" — 3-step process cards
3. "Monitor early indicators of 1000s of diseases" — icon list + circular
   body diagram graphic
4. "160+ lab tests chosen by top doctors" — category card grid (Hormones,
   Cancer, Heart, Aging, Mental health, +More)
5. "The new standard for health" — four stacked photographic panels
6. Press logo row (WSJ, NYT, VOGUE, CNBC)
7. "Real people. Real results." — four video-testimonial portrait tiles
8. "Gold standard for lab testing" — stat row (2,000+ partners, 75M+
   something) + comparison table: Function membership column highlighted
   in terracotta vs. competitor columns in grey, row-by-row checkmarks
9. "Built with the world's top doctors" — advisory board headshot grid
   with credentials (MD, MPH, PhD)
10. Pricing block ("$1/day" membership card)
11. FAQ accordion
12. Closing CTA + newsletter + dark/cream footer

## Components/signature
- The terracotta-highlighted comparison table/column is the site's
  signature data-trust device: it visually singles out "Function" against
  competitors row-by-row rather than showing Function's data in isolation.
- Circular "body map" icon graphic used as a lightweight, non-clinical way
  to represent "1000s of diseases monitored" without a literal anatomical
  illustration.
- Doctor advisory board presented with real headshots + full credentials
  (MD/PhD/MPH) directly under the pricing section — credentials placed at
  the moment of purchase decision, not buried in an About page.

## Motion/interactions
- Testimonial tiles are click-to-play video, not autoplay — keeps the page
  performant and calm despite being content-dense.
- Sticky top bar persists plan-inclusion chips while scrolling, reinforcing
  value throughout a long page.

## Biomarker/trust presentation
- Comparison-table format (Function vs. "average checkup") rather than a
  chart or gauge — trust is built by relative positioning against a
  familiar competitor/baseline, not by visualizing a single user's data.
- Clinician credentials (MD, PhD, MPH) shown with headshots directly below
  the product/pricing section.
- Press-logo row and raw member-count stats (2,000+, 75M+) used as social
  proof rather than clinical certification badges.

## What works
- A warm editorial serif + terracotta accent breaks the sterile
  blue/white medical-SaaS cliché while the underlying content (lab test
  categories, doctor credentials, comparison table) stays rigorously
  data-forward — proves "scientific" and "warm/editorial" aren't mutually
  exclusive.
- The row-by-row highlighted comparison table is more persuasive than a
  raw feature list because it's legible at a glance and personalizes the
  claim ("you vs. status quo").

## Avoid
- Light-weight (300) serif at 80px can thin out on lower-quality displays;
  keep body/UI text on the sturdier sans weight for legibility.
- The comparison table pattern requires a credible, named competitor
  baseline to work — without one it can read as an unsubstantiated claim.

## How to apply
- Use a light editorial serif for headlines with italic keyword emphasis,
  paired with a plain grotesk body, over a warm cream/terracotta palette,
  to make a biomarker-testing brand feel considered rather than clinical.
- Replace a generic feature-comparison table with a "you vs. baseline"
  highlighted-column table as the primary conversion device.
